title: On-Policy Self-Training: Data-Free Self-Improvement in Large Language Models

paper.title: On-Policy Self-Training: Data-Free Self-Improvement in Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Abstract On-policy self-distillation enables post-training foundation models without relying on stronger external teachers. However, existing approaches rely on ground-truth question-answer pairs, human-curated problem sets, or other supervised signals. In this work, we reformulate on-policy self-distillation as a self-training framework, driven by self-generated question-answer pairs and privileged reasoning demonstrations. We push supervision to the limit: guided solely by coarse, high-level topic descriptions, the model synthesizes its own curriculum of queries and privileged reasoning traces without access to any human-curated prompts or answers. We find that self-distillation on fully synthetic privileged information enables a model to improve across multiple domains while retaining its capabilities on domains it is not self-trained on. We demonstrate the generality of this framework across text and multimodal domains, achieving consistent self-improvement on standard language benchmarks and Visual Question Answering. Our findings demonstrate that foundation models possess rich latent capabilities that can be amplified without external task supervision or curated problem distributions.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Post-training is a primary driver of capability gains in large language models ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , and its paradigms differ along two axes: whether training trajectories come from the model itself, and how dense the learning signal is. Supervised finetuning (SFT) imitates curated demonstrations, providing dense token-level targets on teacher-forced trajectories the model never visits at inference, which induces exposure bias ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) and erodes existing capabilities ( Shenfeld et al., 2026b ) . Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains on the model’s own rollouts ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) , avoiding this mismatch but compressing supervision into a single scalar per trajectory. On-policy distillation (OPD) combines the two: the student samples its own trajectories, and a teacher supplies dense next-token targets at the states it visits ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) removes the need for a stronger teacher by constructing teacher and student from the same parameters under asymmetric conditioning ( Zhao et al., 2026a ; Shenfeld et al., 2026a ) . Across this progression, external supervision is relocated rather than removed: SFT requires reference solutions, RLVR gold answers, OPD a stronger teacher, and OPSD a privileged context, typically the ground-truth solution. Curating this required supervision at scale is costly: process-level annotation of a single mathematics corpus required about 800,000 human step labels ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) , and open instruction datasets rest on crowdsourcing efforts spanning over 13,000 volunteers ( Köpf et al., 2023 ) . This cost has motivated a shift toward synthetic supervision, in which the model generates its own instructions ( Wang et al., 2023b ) , rationales ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ) , or pseudo-solutions ( Li et al., 2026 ) . However, these methods still start from human-written problems, so human curation still decides which problems the model trains on and, in turn, what it can learn. In language models, self-training is an established approach to self-improvement ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2023 ; Singh et al., 2024 ; Zuo et al., 2025 ) . The model solves problems, filters its solutions by agreement with a reference answer or its own majority vote, and is finetuned on those it retains. These methods, however, still train on a curated problem set, which must be collected anew for every task ( Singh et al., 2024 ) . Yet a language model can pose problems, not only solve the ones it is given ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Therefore, we investigate whether a language model can self-train without labels or a curated problem set, requiring only topic descriptors from which it generates its own training problems. In this work, we propose On-Policy Self-Training (OPST) , an approach to self-train a language model with dense supervision derived from self-generated privileged information (Figure 1 ). We remove both ground-truth answers and the curated problem set: conditioned only on a coarse topic descriptor, the model synthesizes both a query and the privileged information (PI) used to train on it. Since the generated question-answer pairs are no longer human-curated, the quality of this data can be noisy. Hence, we filter the generated data along two axes: Pseudo-verification ensures that a problem is well-formed, requiring the model to reproduce its answer in a fresh context and under a paraphrase. Further, we apply a consensus gate to ensure that the problem is informative, discarding problems whose answer the student already consistently reproduces across on-policy rollouts. Because the gate is evaluated against the current student, the difficulty of the retained curriculum implicitly evolves as the student model improves. On the quality-filtered samples, we train the model with on-policy self-distillation (Figure 2 ), where the teacher provides high-quality token-level supervision to the student, limiting catastrophic forgetting of existing capabilities acquired from supervised data ( Shenfeld et al., 2026b ; Shenfeld et al., 2026a ) . These effects come from only the teacher being conditioned on the privileged information, while the student receives the question alone. This asymmetry is crucial in a purely synthetic setting. SFT on the generated answer, or RL rewarding agreement with it, treats the generated answer as the optimization target, which bounds the supervision by the quality of the generation. We show that providing the synthetic answer as context to the teacher instead enables it to produce a reasoning rollout from its own parametric knowledge that serves as an enriched learning signal to the student. The student’s supervision is therefore extended by what the teacher can infer from the privileged, generated context, exceeding what the generated answer alone provides. Iterating this loop improves the model over successive rounds, while an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher stabilizes against self-induced distribution drift. In our experiments, we show that OPST improves language and multimodal reasoning without human-curated questions or answers, outperforming alternative training strategies. On Gemma 4 E2B ( Gemma Team et al., 2026 ) , self-training increases MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021a ) accuracy by + 10.2 +10.2 points, with consistent gains on GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , GPQA ( Rein et al., 2024 ) , and HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) . We also find that self-training in-domain transfers to out-of-distribution domains, with performance either remaining stable or also improving. Applied to vision-language models with unlabeled images alone, Visual OPST improves VQAv2 accuracy by + 6.9 +6.9 points. Figure 1: On-Policy Self-Training loop. Seeded only by topic descriptors, the model generates and filters its own question-answer pairs, then trains on them via on-policy self-distillation from a privileged EMA teacher, iterating for data-free self-improvement.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: On-policy self-distillation. OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) constructs both policies from a single model, conditioning the teacher on a verified reference solution. Since on-policy methods train on the model’s own samples, they forget less than SFT ( Shenfeld et al., 2026b ) , and self-distillation has been shown to enable continual learning across multiple domains ( Shenfeld et al., 2026a ) . Subsequent work varies the privileged context between expert demonstrations ( Shenfeld et al., 2026a ) , privileged observations ( Penaloza et al., 2026 ) , and environmental feedback ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . Others address information leakage and instability ( Yang et al., 2026 ) or extend the setting to agentic tasks ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Closest to our work, Li et al. (2026) replace the gold solution with a majority-vote consensus over the model’s own rollouts, eliminating answer supervision. All of these, however, operate on a given distribution of problems. OPST removes that assumption: the model synthesizes its own queries from a coarse topic descriptor, so neither the problems nor their solutions are externally supplied. LLM Self-Training. Early self-training methods filter solutions by agreement with a reference answer ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ; Singh et al., 2024 ) or by self-consistency across samples ( Huang et al., 2023 ) , and label-free reinforcement learning has since replaced the reference answer with majority votes ( Zuo et al., 2025 ) or the model’s own confidence ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) . These methods remove answers but not problems: each still trains on a curated problem set, which must be collected anew for every task ( Singh et al., 2024 ) . Self-play methods let a proposer generate tasks, seeded by as little as a topic description and checked by a code executor or by majority voting over the solver’s answers ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Self-generated problems, however, carry information that self-play reduces to a scalar reward: the answer and rationale the model produces while posing them. Used as privileged context for a self-distillation teacher, it instead yields dense, token-level supervision. On curated problems, Li et al. (2026) show that self-generated answers are considerably more effective as teacher context than as a reward, and Zhang et al. (2026) combine self-play with self-distillation for search agents. While their method requires no external training data, question construction is grounded in documents retrieved from an external corpus, whereas OPST generates problems from the model’s parametric knowledge alone. Whether a model can improve from problems it poses itself, with dense token-level supervision and without retrieval or other external grounding, has to our knowledge not yet been studied for general reasoning. Figure 2: Model training. As in OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) , the student sees only the question and matches the next-token distribution of a teacher that also sees privileged information. In OPST, this information is self-generated, and the teacher is an EMA of the student.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: In this section, we present On-Policy Self-Training. We first define the data-free post-training setting (Section 3.1 ) and review on-policy self-distillation (Section 3.2 ). Following, we describe how the model generates problems and privileged information from topic descriptors (Section 3.3 ), how it filters them intrinsically (Section 3.4 ), and how it trains on the result (Section 3.5 ). Repeating these steps yields multiple rounds of self-training (Section 3.6 ). Finally, we extend OPST to vision-language models (Section 3.7 ).

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Formulation: Data-Free Post-Training
sections.text: Post-training typically relies on a curated dataset of human-written queries and ground-truth answers 𝒟 = { ( x i , y i ∗ ) } \mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i}^{*})\} , or at least on a curated prompt distribution 𝒟 prompts = { x i } \mathcal{D}_{\text{prompts}}=\{x_{i}\} . In data-free post-training , neither is available. Training is seeded only by a set of coarse topic descriptors 𝒯 = { τ 1 , … , τ K } \mathcal{T}=\{\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{K}\} , where each τ k \tau_{k} names a broad subject area, such as “Abstract Algebra” or “Commonsense Causal Reasoning” . From 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , the model generates a synthetic training set 𝒟 syn = { ( x i , z i ) } i = 1 N \mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}=\{(x_{i},z_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} , where x i x_{i} is a generated query and z i z_{i} its privileged information, consisting of a rationale and a candidate answer (Section 3.3 ). The setting has two objectives. First, the model must improve its reasoning in the seeded domains using only self-generated problems and privileged information. Second, because the training signal comes from its own generations without human oversight, the model must retain its general reasoning and previously acquired parametric knowledge on domains it is not self-trained on, a prerequisite for repeating the process over multiple rounds.

sections.text: On-policy self-distillation ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) derives the student π θ \pi_{\theta} and the teacher π ϕ \pi_{\phi} from the same model and replaces the capability gap of standard distillation ( Kim & Rush, 2016 ) with an information gap. Given a problem x x , the student samples a response y = ( y 1 , … , y T ) ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) , with next-token distribution p t = π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , y < t ) p_{t}=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}) (1) at step t t . The teacher evaluates the same prefix y < t y_{<t} , but is additionally conditioned on privileged information z z that the student does not see: q t = π ϕ ( ⋅ ∣ x , z , y < t ) . q_{t}=\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid x,z,y_{<t}). (2) The student is trained to match the teacher along its own trajectory, ℒ OPSD ( θ ) = 𝔼 ( x , z ) ∼ 𝒟 , y ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) [ 1 ∑ t M t ∑ t = 1 T M t D ( p t ∥ q t ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\text{OPSD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,z)\sim\mathcal{D},\;y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\frac{1}{\sum_{t}M_{t}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}M_{t}\,D(p_{t}\,\|\,q_{t})\right], (3) where D D is a divergence between distributions, M t ∈ { 0 , 1 } M_{t}\in\{0,1\} masks padding tokens, and no gradient flows through the teacher. In standard OPSD, z z is a reference solution ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) . Existing OPSD methods, however, assume a curated problem set and typically use a reference solution as z z . The following sections describe how OPST generates both with the model itself.

sections.heading: 3.3 Topic-Seeded Curriculum Generation
sections.text: Instead of drawing problems from a curated distribution, OPST generates them from the topic descriptors 𝒯 \mathcal{T} . Given a topic τ ∈ 𝒯 \tau\in\mathcal{T} , a generator π gen \pi_{\text{gen}} produces a query x x together with privileged information z z , ( x , z ) ∼ π gen ( ⋅ ∣ τ ) , z = ( r , a ) , (x,z)\sim\pi_{\text{gen}}(\cdot\mid\tau),\quad z=(r,a), (4) where r r is a rationale and a a a candidate answer. Queries can be multiple-choice or open-ended, and we sample at temperature T gen T_{\text{gen}} to obtain diverse problems. While the student receives the query x x alone, the teacher also receives z z as additional privileged information. We embed the topic name into a targeted data generation prompt, asking the model to pose problems on the given topic along with generated privileged information. In practice, the model generates partial or full answers to the posed problem. Where available, topics are data-domain category labels. The applied prompt templates are provided in Appendix A.7 . We instantiate π gen \pi_{\text{gen}} either as the EMA teacher π ϕ \pi_{\phi} (Section 3.5 ), so that data quality can improve as training progresses, or as a frozen copy of the initial model π θ 0 \pi_{\theta_{0}} . The student does not generate data, but its rollouts determine which samples are retained (Section 3.4 ).

sections.heading: 3.4 Pseudo-Verification & Consensus Gate
sections.text: Removing human supervision removes not only human data curation but also quality assurance. Generated samples can contain ill-posed questions or incorrect candidate answers, and training on them propagates these errors. At the same time, not every well-posed sample is worth training on: if the student already solves a problem reliably, the teacher conditioned on z z produces nearly the same next-token distribution as the student, and the sample contributes little beyond its generation and rollout cost. We therefore filter any generated sample for two criteria: Pseudo-verification first estimates whether a sample is well-formed, and the consensus gate then approximates whether it is informative for the current student.

sections.heading: Pseudo-Verification.
sections.text: We evaluate if a given generated sample possesses two properties of a well-posed problem: its answer should be reproducible without the generator’s own intent as context, and it should not depend on the particular wording of the question. To pseudo-verify the generated answer, we require the generator to recover it when solving the question in a fresh context, without access to z z and at a low temperature, which yields a ^ ​ ( x ) = a \hat{a}(x)=a . This separates authoring from solving: when query and answer are generated in one pass, a flawed or ambiguous question can still receive a confident answer. To pseudo-verify the generated problem statement, we prompt the generator to paraphrase x x into x ′ ∼ π gen ( ⋅ ∣ x ) x^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\text{gen}}(\cdot\mid x) with an instruction to preserve its meaning, solve x ′ x^{\prime} under the same conditions, and require the answer to be unchanged, a ^ ​ ( x ′ ) = a \hat{a}(x^{\prime})=a . A well-posed question has the same answer regardless of its wording, so this rejects questions whose answer depends on incidental phrasing, which typically indicates that the question admits more than one reading. sections.heading: Consensus Gate.
sections.text: We assume that the samples that carry the most signal are those the student cannot yet answer reliably: a question that is trivial for the student yields the same answer on every rollout, and the privileged teacher has little to add. We therefore measure answer agreement across sampled reasoning paths as in self-consistency ( Wang et al., 2023a ) . For each verified sample, the student samples G G rollouts { y g } g = 1 G ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) \{y_{g}\}_{g=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) , from which we extract answers { a ^ g } g = 1 G \{\hat{a}_{g}\}_{g=1}^{G} . Samples with full agreement with the candidate answer, c ( x , z ) = 1 G ∑ g = 1 G 𝕀 [ a ^ g = a ] = 1 c(x,z)=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\mathbb{I}[\hat{a}_{g}=a]=1 , provide little new signal for the model and are discarded. The two filters act in opposite directions by design. Pseudo-verification keeps samples that are stable enough for the generated answer to serve as privileged information, while the consensus gate discards samples the student already solves. The retained samples therefore lie at the student’s capability frontier, and since the gate depends on the current student, the difficulty of the curriculum evolves with the model.

sections.heading: EMA Teacher.
sections.text: The teacher is initialized from the student, ϕ 0 = θ 0 \phi_{0}=\theta_{0} , and updated after every gradient step as ϕ k = ( 1 − β ) ​ ϕ k − 1 + β ​ θ k \phi_{k}=(1-\beta)\,\phi_{k-1}+\beta\,\theta_{k} . Since the teacher produces the dense supervision, it must remain stable. With β = 1 \beta=1 , a single noisy batch immediately changes the targets for subsequent batches, and errors can reinforce themselves. The EMA instead averages out such fluctuations over roughly 1 / β 1/\beta steps. Averaging the student’s weights also yields a more accurate model than the student itself (Table 6 d), consistent with momentum teachers in vision ( Caron et al., 2021 ) . For this reason, the teacher is the model we evaluate.

sections.heading: 3.6 Iterative Self-Training
sections.text: A single round of OPST is limited by the quality of the data and supervision that the initial model provides. We therefore repeat generation, verification, and training over N N rounds. The student and teacher weights carry over from one round to the next. For each additional round, π gen \pi_{\text{gen}} generates a new training set, from which we remove problems that duplicate those of earlier rounds. The iterative nature of our loop lets student and teacher co-evolve. Training on new data further improves the student, and through the EMA update, also the teacher. A stronger teacher, in turn, benefits the next round in three ways. It provides more accurate token-level targets on the student’s rollouts. As the generator, it produces better problems and privileged information. And as the verifier (Section 3.4 ), it judges its own data more reliably, so fewer incorrect samples reach training. Because the teacher is an average over many training steps, only improvements that persist across batches enter this cycle.

sections.heading: 3.7 Visual OPST
sections.text: OPST is modality-agnostic and can be extended to the multimodal setting by adding an unlabeled modality. We therefore explore this for vision-language tasks by adding images to the process. Visual OPST uses a collection of unlabeled images ℐ \mathcal{I} and visual topic descriptors 𝒯 vis \mathcal{T}_{\text{vis}} , such as “Spatial Relations” , “Object Counting” , or “Attribute Recognition” . Unlike the text setting, it requires unlabeled images as input, from which we generate the same data as detailed in Section 3.3 .

sections.text: Given an image I ∈ ℐ I\in\mathcal{I} and a topic τ ∈ 𝒯 vis \tau\in\mathcal{T}_{\text{vis}} , the generator produces a question about the image together with privileged information, ( x , z ) ∼ π gen ( ⋅ ∣ I , τ ) (x,z)\sim\pi_{\text{gen}}(\cdot\mid I,\tau) . We consider two forms of privileged information. In the first, z z is a detailed scene caption that the generator writes for I I , describing its objects, attributes, and spatial arrangement. In the second, we prompt the model to detect the objects in the scene, from which we bootstrap bounding-box grounded spatial relations. The privileged caption informs the teacher rollout with explicit visual details that the student must extract from the image itself, while the detected spatial relations help ground the teacher with actual object positions. Both forms can be combined by conditioning the teacher on the caption and the spatial relations.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Our experimental evaluation focuses on three aspects: in-domain self-improvement without human-curated data, knowledge retention on out-of-domain (OOD) benchmarks when mixing data generation domains, and transfer to multimodal inputs with Visual OPST.

sections.heading: Models and Datasets.
sections.text: As base models, we utilize the Gemma 4 E2B and E4B models ( Gemma Team et al., 2026 ) . Data Generation is seeded with topic descriptors covering the domains of four in-domain benchmarks: MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021a ) , GPQA ( Rein et al., 2024 ) , GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , and HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) . To measure transfer and retention, we additionally evaluate on three OOD benchmarks that no topic descriptor targets: ARC-Challenge ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , MATH-500 ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Hendrycks et al., 2021b ) , and Winogrande ( Sakaguchi et al., 2021 ) . For the multi-domain experiments (Table 3 ), GPQA is treated as out-of-domain.

sections.text: On Gemma 4 E2B without thinking, OPST improves MMLU by + 10.2 +10.2 points, GPQA by + 4.0 +4.0 , and HellaSwag by + 7.5 +7.5 (Table 1 ). sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced On-Policy Self-Training (OPST), which post-trains a model on self-generated problems and privileged information, seeded only by coarse topic descriptors. We showed that conditioning the teacher on the generated answer, rather than training on it, lets the teacher fill in omitted reasoning steps and limits the influence of potentially noisy data. We found that OPST outperforms SFT and GRPO on the same generated data and methods that rely on curated questions, and extends to multiple domains and vision-language models, demonstrating that models can self-improve from self-generated data alone.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: OPST can only amplify existing knowledge, and since pseudo-verification measures self-consistency rather than correctness, consistent errors still enter training. Our topic descriptors are hand-chosen, and our experiments are limited to small models. Promising directions include label-free stopping criteria and tool- or retrieval-grounded verification.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: In this work, we used generative AI tools for implementing training infrastructure and experiment scripts and for feedback on the experimental design. We have not used generative AI tools for generating core research ideas, formulating hypotheses, or modifying evaluation benchmark data, and tasks involving human-subject data are not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools for drafting and editing parts of the manuscript, improving readability, checking and formatting tables, plotting utilities, and debugging LaTeX compilation. Open-weight generative models (Gemma 4) serve as the primary object of study and generate the synthetic training data within our proposed self-training pipeline. sections.heading: A.1 Self-Distillation Objectives on Generated Data.
sections.text: Unlike a ground-truth reference solution, generated privileged information z = ( r , a ) z=(r,a) can be ambiguous: the rationale r r may miss important aspects, and the candidate answer a a may be partially or fully incorrect. Therefore, training a model on z z directly inherits these defects. SFT on the generated pairs maximizes log ⁡ π θ ​ ( z ∣ x ) = ∑ j = 1 | z | log ⁡ π θ ​ ( z j ∣ x , z < j ) , \log\pi_{\theta}(z\mid x)=\sum_{j=1}^{|z|}\log\pi_{\theta}(z_{j}\mid x,z_{<j}), (8) which supervises the model only on the tokens of z z . Critically, it treats every token as correct, including any potential omissions and errors. OPSD instead uses z z as context: at every state y < t y_{<t} the student visits, the teacher supplies a full next-token distribution, so supervision covers the entire student rollout rather than the | z | |z| tokens of the generation. Crucially, the teacher produces this rollout from its own knowledge under the exposure to the generated privileged information. This leads to a more nuanced, higher-quality supervision, since the teacher reweights the model’s own next-token distribution by how consistent each continuation is with the privileged information. This has three consequences for generated data. First, z z need not spell out a step for the teacher to supervise it: tokens that move the rollout toward a a are upweighted, so the teacher completes reasoning that r r omits. Second, the target is expressed in the model’s own distribution rather than in the surface form of z z , so the student does not imitate the phrasing or formatting of the generation. Third, the prior limits the influence of a faulty z z : an error shifts the target only to the extent that the model finds it plausible, and where the prior favors a different step, the teacher retains that step instead of copying the error. The student therefore learns from what the model can infer given z z as a hint, not from z z itself. Consequently, conditioning the teacher on z z yields dense, prior-grounded token-level supervision that filters generation noise, making on-policy self-distillation well suited for learning from purely synthetic data.

sections.heading: EMA Update.
sections.text: The EMA teacher is meant to provide stable targets despite noisy updates on generated data (Section 3.5 ). We vary its rate β \beta (Table 6 a). Without an EMA ( β = 1 \beta=1 ), the teacher follows the student’s current weights, and OPST barely improves over the base model ( 38.1 38.1 vs. 37.5 37.5 ). Too much smoothing also slows progress: with β = 0.01 \beta=0.01 , the teacher incorporates the student’s improvements too slowly and reaches 45.2 45.2 , whereas β = 0.05 \beta=0.05 performs best ( 47.7 47.7 ).

sections.heading: Dataset Size per Round.
sections.text: The number of samples per round trades off the amount of data against how often the improving teacher regenerates it. We vary it from 57 57 to 570 570 samples (Table 6 b). Accuracy increases up to 285 285 samples and then saturates, decreasing slightly to 46.9 46.9 at 570 570 samples. Larger rounds therefore add generation cost without improving results.

sections.heading: Number of Rounds.
sections.text: Iterating lets student and teacher improve each other, but errors in the generated data can also accumulate over rounds (Section 3.6 ). We evaluate the model after different numbers of rounds (Table 6 c). Significant improvements emerge after the first three rounds ( + 5.6 +5.6 ), and accuracy is highest after seven rounds ( 47.7 47.7 ). Further rounds bring no additional improvement, but performance remains stable at around 46 46 , well above the base model.

sections.text: Because the EMA teacher averages over the student’s recent updates, it may also be the better model to deploy. We compare the student and the EMA teacher at the end of training (Table 6 d). The EMA teacher is 1.8 1.8 points more accurate, consistent with the student’s weights being affected by noise from recent batches that averaging removes.

sections.heading: A.6 Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: We follow the task formulations of the EleutherAI lm-evaluation-harness ( Gao et al., 2023 ) and adapt them to the Gemma 4 chat template. Without thinking, we score all multiple-choice benchmarks, i.e., MMLU, GPQA Diamond, HellaSwag, ARC-Challenge, and Winogrande, by log-likelihood over the closed set of answer options. No answer is therefore parsed from generated text. We use the harness defaults, i.e., 5-shot prompting for MMLU, zero-shot prompting for the remaining multiple-choice benchmarks, and length-normalized accuracy where the harness specifies it. GSM8K is evaluated with 8-shot chain-of-thought prompting ( Wei et al., 2022 ) . With thinking, multiple-choice answers are parsed from the final Answer: X line. GSM8K is graded by exact match of the final numerical answer, and MATH-500 by symbolic equivalence of the final \boxed{} expression using SymPy. For all models and benchmarks, both before and after self-training, the rate of parsing failures and invalid answers is 0%. Performance differences in the thinking regime therefore do not stem from changes in answer formatting. All remaining settings follow the harness defaults.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.32770v1 [cs.CL] 23 Oct 2026 On-Policy Self-Training: Data-Free Self-Improvement in Large Language Models Leon Sick 1,2, ∗ \ast Lukas Hoyer 1 Yannick Strümpler 1 Christian Reisswig 1 Affiliation: Timo Ropinski 2 Federico Tombari 1 Affiliation: 1 Google 2 Ulm University Abstract On-policy self-distillation enables post-training foundation models without relying on stronger external teachers. However, existing approaches rely on ground-truth question-answer pairs, human-curated problem sets, or other supervised signals. In this work, we reformulate on-policy self-distillation as a self-training framework, driven by self-generated question-answer pairs and privileged reasoning demonstrations. We push supervision to the limit: guided solely by coarse, high-level topic descriptions, the model synthesizes its own curriculum of queries and privileged reasoning traces without access to any human-curated prompts or answers. We find that self-distillation on fully synthetic privileged information enables a model to improve across multiple domains while retaining its capabilities on domains it is not self-trained on. We demonstrate the generality of this framework across text and multimodal domains, achieving consistent self-improvement on standard language benchmarks and Visual Question Answering. Our findings demonstrate that foundation models possess rich latent capabilities that can be amplified without external task supervision or curated problem distributions. $\ast$ $\ast$ footnotetext: Work done during an internship at Google. 1 Introduction Post-training is a primary driver of capability gains in large language models ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , and its paradigms differ along two axes: whether training trajectories come from the model itself, and how dense the learning signal is. Supervised finetuning (SFT) imitates curated demonstrations, providing dense token-level targets on teacher-forced trajectories the model never visits at inference, which induces exposure bias ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) and erodes existing capabilities ( Shenfeld et al., 2026b ) . Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains on the model’s own rollouts ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) , avoiding this mismatch but compressing supervision into a single scalar per trajectory. On-policy distillation (OPD) combines the two: the student samples its own trajectories, and a teacher supplies dense next-token targets at the states it visits ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) . On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) removes the need for a stronger teacher by constructing teacher and student from the same parameters under asymmetric conditioning ( Zhao et al., 2026a ; Shenfeld et al., 2026a ) . Across this progression, external supervision is relocated rather than removed: SFT requires reference solutions, RLVR gold answers, OPD a stronger teacher, and OPSD a privileged context, typically the ground-truth solution. Curating this required supervision at scale is costly: process-level annotation of a single mathematics corpus required about 800,000 human step labels ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) , and open instruction datasets rest on crowdsourcing efforts spanning over 13,000 volunteers ( Köpf et al., 2023 ) . This cost has motivated a shift toward synthetic supervision, in which the model generates its own instructions ( Wang et al., 2023b ) , rationales ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ) , or pseudo-solutions ( Li et al., 2026 ) . However, these methods still start from human-written problems, so human curation still decides which problems the model trains on and, in turn, what it can learn. In language models, self-training is an established approach to self-improvement ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2023 ; Singh et al., 2024 ; Zuo et al., 2025 ) . The model solves problems, filters its solutions by agreement with a reference answer or its own majority vote, and is finetuned on those it retains. These methods, however, still train on a curated problem set, which must be collected anew for every task ( Singh et al., 2024 ) . Yet a language model can pose problems, not only solve the ones it is given ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Therefore, we investigate whether a language model can self-train without labels or a curated problem set, requiring only topic descriptors from which it generates its own training problems. In this work, we propose On-Policy Self-Training (OPST) , an approach to self-train a language model with dense supervision derived from self-generated privileged information (Figure 1 ). We remove both ground-truth answers and the curated problem set: conditioned only on a coarse topic descriptor, the model synthesizes both a query and the privileged information (PI) used to train on it. Since the generated question-answer pairs are no longer human-curated, the quality of this data can be noisy. Hence, we filter the generated data along two axes: Pseudo-verification ensures that a problem is well-formed, requiring the model to reproduce its answer in a fresh context and under a paraphrase. Further, we apply a consensus gate to ensure that the problem is informative, discarding problems whose answer the student already consistently reproduces across on-policy rollouts. Because the gate is evaluated against the current student, the difficulty of the retained curriculum implicitly evolves as the student model improves. On the quality-filtered samples, we train the model with on-policy self-distillation (Figure 2 ), where the teacher provides high-quality token-level supervision to the student, limiting catastrophic forgetting of existing capabilities acquired from supervised data ( Shenfeld et al., 2026b ; Shenfeld et al., 2026a ) . These effects come from only the teacher being conditioned on the privileged information, while the student receives the question alone. This asymmetry is crucial in a purely synthetic setting. SFT on the generated answer, or RL rewarding agreement with it, treats the generated answer as the optimization target, which bounds the supervision by the quality of the generation. We show that providing the synthetic answer as context to the teacher instead enables it to produce a reasoning rollout from its own parametric knowledge that serves as an enriched learning signal to the student. The student’s supervision is therefore extended by what the teacher can infer from the privileged, generated context, exceeding what the generated answer alone provides. Iterating this loop improves the model over successive rounds, while an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher stabilizes against self-induced distribution drift. In our experiments, we show that OPST improves language and multimodal reasoning without human-curated questions or answers, outperforming alternative training strategies. On Gemma 4 E2B ( Gemma Team et al., 2026 ) , self-training increases MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021a ) accuracy by + 10.2 +10.2 points, with consistent gains on GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , GPQA ( Rein et al., 2024 ) , and HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) . We also find that self-training in-domain transfers to out-of-distribution domains, with performance either remaining stable or also improving. Applied to vision-language models with unlabeled images alone, Visual OPST improves VQAv2 accuracy by + 6.9 +6.9 points. Figure 1: On-Policy Self-Training loop. Seeded only by topic descriptors, the model generates and filters its own question-answer pairs, then trains on them via on-policy self-distillation from a privileged EMA teacher, iterating for data-free self-improvement. 2 Related Work On-policy self-distillation. OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) constructs both policies from a single model, conditioning the teacher on a verified reference solution. Since on-policy methods train on the model’s own samples, they forget less than SFT ( Shenfeld et al., 2026b ) , and self-distillation has been shown to enable continual learning across multiple domains ( Shenfeld et al., 2026a ) . Subsequent work varies the privileged context between expert demonstrations ( Shenfeld et al., 2026a ) , privileged observations ( Penaloza et al., 2026 ) , and environmental feedback ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) . Others address information leakage and instability ( Yang et al., 2026 ) or extend the setting to agentic tasks ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Closest to our work, Li et al. (2026) replace the gold solution with a majority-vote consensus over the model’s own rollouts, eliminating answer supervision. All of these, however, operate on a given distribution of problems. OPST removes that assumption: the model synthesizes its own queries from a coarse topic descriptor, so neither the problems nor their solutions are externally supplied. LLM Self-Training. Early self-training methods filter solutions by agreement with a reference answer ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ; Singh et al., 2024 ) or by self-consistency across samples ( Huang et al., 2023 ) , and label-free reinforcement learning has since replaced the reference answer with majority votes ( Zuo et al., 2025 ) or the model’s own confidence ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) . These methods remove answers but not problems: each still trains on a curated problem set, which must be collected anew for every task ( Singh et al., 2024 ) . Self-play methods let a proposer generate tasks, seeded by as little as a topic description and checked by a code executor or by majority voting over the solver’s answers ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Self-generated problems, however, carry information that self-play reduces to a scalar reward: the answer and rationale the model produces while posing them. Used as privileged context for a self-distillation teacher, it instead yields dense, token-level supervision. On curated problems, Li et al. (2026) show that self-generated answers are considerably more effective as teacher context than as a reward, and Zhang et al. (2026) combine self-play with self-distillation for search agents. While their method requires no external training data, question construction is grounded in documents retrieved from an external corpus, whereas OPST generates problems from the model’s parametric knowledge alone. Whether a model can improve from problems it poses itself, with dense token-level supervision and without retrieval or other external grounding, has to our knowledge not yet been studied for general reasoning. Figure 2: Model training. As in OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) , the student sees only the question and matches the next-token distribution of a teacher that also sees privileged information. In OPST, this information is self-generated, and the teacher is an EMA of the student. 3 Method In this section, we present On-Policy Self-Training. We first define the data-free post-training setting (Section 3.1 ) and review on-policy self-distillation (Section 3.2 ). Following, we describe how the model generates problems and privileged information from topic descriptors (Section 3.3 ), how it filters them intrinsically (Section 3.4 ), and how it trains on the result (Section 3.5 ). Repeating these steps yields multiple rounds of self-training (Section 3.6 ). Finally, we extend OPST to vision-language models (Section 3.7 ). 3.1 Problem Formulation: Data-Free Post-Training Post-training typically relies on a curated dataset of human-written queries and ground-truth answers 𝒟 = { ( x i , y i ∗ ) } \mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},y_{i}^{*})\} , or at least on a curated prompt distribution 𝒟 prompts = { x i } \mathcal{D}_{\text{prompts}}=\{x_{i}\} . In data-free post-training , neither is available. Training is seeded only by a set of coarse topic descriptors 𝒯 = { τ 1 , … , τ K } \mathcal{T}=\{\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{K}\} , where each τ k \tau_{k} names a broad subject area, such as “Abstract Algebra” or “Commonsense Causal Reasoning” . From 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , the model generates a synthetic training set 𝒟 syn = { ( x i , z i ) } i = 1 N \mathcal{D}_{\text{syn}}=\{(x_{i},z_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} , where x i x_{i} is a generated query and z i z_{i} its privileged information, consisting of a rationale and a candidate answer (Section 3.3 ). The setting has two objectives. First, the model must improve its reasoning in the seeded domains using only self-generated problems and privileged information. Second, because the training signal comes from its own generations without human oversight, the model must retain its general reasoning and previously acquired parametric knowledge on domains it is not self-trained on, a prerequisite for repeating the process over multiple rounds. 3.2 Preliminaries: On-Policy Self-Distillation On-policy self-distillation ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) derives the student π θ \pi_{\theta} and the teacher π ϕ \pi_{\phi} from the same model and replaces the capability gap of standard distillation ( Kim & Rush, 2016 ) with an information gap. Given a problem x x , the student samples a response y = ( y 1 , … , y T ) ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) y=(y_{1},\dots,y_{T})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) , with next-token distribution p t = π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , y < t ) p_{t}=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}) (1) at step t t . The teacher evaluates the same prefix y < t y_{<t} , but is additionally conditioned on privileged information z z that the student does not see: q t = π ϕ ( ⋅ ∣ x , z , y < t ) . q_{t}=\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid x,z,y_{<t}). (2) The student is trained to match the teacher along its own trajectory, ℒ OPSD ( θ ) = 𝔼 ( x , z ) ∼ 𝒟 , y ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) [ 1 ∑ t M t ∑ t = 1 T M t D ( p t ∥ q t ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\text{OPSD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(x,z)\sim\mathcal{D},\;y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\frac{1}{\sum_{t}M_{t}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}M_{t}\,D(p_{t}\,\|\,q_{t})\right], (3) where D D is a divergence between distributions, M t ∈ { 0 , 1 } M_{t}\in\{0,1\} masks padding tokens, and no gradient flows through the teacher. In standard OPSD, z z is a reference solution ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) . Existing OPSD methods, however, assume a curated problem set and typically use a reference solution as z z . The following sections describe how OPST generates both with the model itself. 3.3 Topic-Seeded Curriculum Generation Instead of drawing problems from a curated distribution, OPST generates them from the topic descriptors 𝒯 \mathcal{T} . Given a topic τ ∈ 𝒯 \tau\in\mathcal{T} , a generator π gen \pi_{\text{gen}} produces a query x x together with privileged information z z , ( x , z ) ∼ π gen ( ⋅ ∣ τ ) , z = ( r , a ) , (x,z)\sim\pi_{\text{gen}}(\cdot\mid\tau),\quad z=(r,a), (4) where r r is a rationale and a a a candidate answer. Queries can be multiple-choice or open-ended, and we sample at temperature T gen T_{\text{gen}} to obtain diverse problems. While the student receives the query x x alone, the teacher also receives z z as additional privileged information. We embed the topic name into a targeted data generation prompt, asking the model to pose problems on the given topic along with generated privileged information. Generated samples can contain ill-posed questions or incorrect candidate answers, and training on them propagates these errors. At the same time, not every well-posed sample is worth training on: if the student already solves a problem reliably, the teacher conditioned on z z produces nearly the same next-token distribution as the student, and the sample contributes little beyond its generation and rollout cost. We therefore filter any generated sample for two criteria: Pseudo-verification first estimates whether a sample is well-formed, and the consensus gate then approximates whether it is informative for the current student. We evaluate if a given generated sample possesses two properties of a well-posed problem: its answer should be reproducible without the generator’s own intent as context, and it should not depend on the particular wording of the question. This separates authoring from solving: when query and answer are generated in one pass, a flawed or ambiguous question can still receive a confident answer. Further ablations are provided in Appendix A.2 . 6 Conclusion We introduced On-Policy Self-Training (OPST), which post-trains a model on self-generated problems and privileged information, seeded only by coarse topic descriptors. We showed that conditioning the teacher on the generated answer, rather than training on it, lets the teacher fill in omitted reasoning steps and limits the influence of potentially noisy data. We found that OPST outperforms SFT and GRPO on the same generated data and methods that rely on curated questions, and extends to multiple domains and vision-language models, demonstrating that models can self-improve from self-generated data alone. Limitations. OPST can only amplify existing knowledge, and since pseudo-verification measures self-consistency rather than correctness, consistent errors still enter training. Our topic descriptors are hand-chosen, and our experiments are limited to small models. Promising directions include label-free stopping criteria and tool- or retrieval-grounded verification. Unlike a ground-truth reference solution, generated privileged information z = ( r , a ) z=(r,a) can be ambiguous: the rationale r r may miss important aspects, and the candidate answer a a may be partially or fully incorrect. Therefore, training a model on z z directly inherits these defects. SFT on the generated pairs maximizes log ⁡ π θ ​ ( z ∣ x ) = ∑ j = 1 | z | log ⁡ π θ ​ ( z j ∣ x , z < j ) , \log\pi_{\theta}(z\mid x)=\sum_{j=1}^{|z|}\log\pi_{\theta}(z_{j}\mid x,z_{<j}), (8) which supervises the model only on the tokens of z z . Critically, it treats every token as correct, including any potential omissions and errors. OPSD instead uses z z as context: at every state y < t y_{<t} the student visits, the teacher supplies a full next-token distribution, so supervision covers the entire student rollout rather than the | z | |z| tokens of the generation. Crucially, the teacher produces this rollout from its own knowledge under the exposure to the generated privileged information. This leads to a more nuanced, higher-quality supervision, since the teacher reweights the model’s own next-token distribution by how consistent each continuation is with the privileged information. This has three consequences for generated data. First, z z need not spell out a step for the teacher to supervise it: tokens that move the rollout toward a a are upweighted, so the teacher completes reasoning that r r omits. Second, the target is expressed in the model’s own distribution rather than in the surface form of z z , so the student does not imitate the phrasing or formatting of the generation. Third, the prior limits the influence of a faulty z z : an error shifts the target only to the extent that the model finds it plausible, and where the prior favors a different step, the teacher retains that step instead of copying the error. The student therefore learns from what the model can infer given z z as a hint, not from z z itself. Consequently, conditioning the teacher on z z yields dense, prior-grounded token-level supervision that filters generation noise, making on-policy self-distillation well suited for learning from purely synthetic data.
